item.title: Kubernetes v1.38 introduces breaking changes to WebSockets, cgroup drivers, and kubeconfig APIs
item.description:
Kubernetes v1.38 introduces breaking changes to WebSockets, cgroup drivers, and kubeconfig APIs

As the Kubernetes community approaches the v1.38 release, several deprecated features are being removed or deprecated to improve the project’s long-term health and maintainability. These changes affect kubectl behavior, cgroup configuration, and API stability, requiring cluster administrators to update their configurations and scripts.

📡 Kubectl WebSockets Transition

Kubernetes has progressively moved kubectl from SPDY to WebSockets for exec, attach, and port-forward operations:

Version WebSocket Support
v1.30 Default for exec, attach, cp operations
v1.31 Default for port-forward operations

The environment variables KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS and KUBECTL_PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS were introduced to disable WebSocket usage. In v1.38, these variables will be removed. kubectl will always prefer WebSockets and fall back to SPDY when necessary. Scripts or CI environments that set these variables can remove them as they will no longer have any effect.

⚙️ Kubeconfig API Changes

The kuberc file manages kubectl user preferences and credential plugin allowlists. In the beta kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 API, the name field served as an alias for command. The name field was deprecated in v1.36. With kuberc graduating to stable in v1.38, the new kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1 API will not include name. Users with allowlist entries using name should update them to use command.

🔧 Container Runtime and cgroup Driver Updates

Support for cgroup v1 is being phased out. Since v1.35, kubelet fails to start on cgroup v1 nodes unless failCgroupV1: false is set in the kubelet configuration. This option remains in v1.38 but should be treated as a short-term workaround. Users are encouraged to migrate to cgroup v2.

Additionally, the legacy cgroup driver configuration mechanism is being deprecated. The kubelet will default to not allowing this mechanism in v1.38 and will require the container runtime to be running to query the recommended cgroup driver via CRI RuntimeConfig RPC. If the kubelet cannot retrieve the cgroup driver from the runtime after retrying, it will exit with an error before registering the node. The cgroupDriver field in the kubelet configuration file will be deprecated, and specifying it will be rejected unless the LegacyCgroupDriverFallback feature gate is enabled.

kubeadm will no longer default cgroupDriver to systemd and will report an error during preflight checks if the runtime doesn’t support the RPC.

🌐 Admission Webhook Behavior Changes

Since v1.37, the ExcludeAdmissionWebhookVirtualResources feature gate is enabled by default. With this gate active, validating and mutating admission webhooks no longer receive requests for virtual resources like TokenReview, SelfSubjectReview, SubjectAccessReview, SelfSubjectAccessReview, and LocalSubjectAccessReview. Creating or updating a webhook configuration targeting these resources triggers a deprecation warning. Users relying on webhooks for these requests can disable the gate temporarily, but it is planned to be locked on when the feature graduates to stable.

💾 Resource Limit Enforcement for cgroup v2

On Linux nodes using cgroup v2 and configured with LimitedSwap, v1.38’s kubelet will begin applying swap limits based on the Pod’s memory settings.

🚀 Availability

These changes are planned for the Kubernetes v1.38 release. The information reflects the current status and may change before the actual release date.

#Kubernetes #Containers #cgroups #Kubectl

Source: Kubernetes v1.38 Sneak Peek

item.title: New AI Development Tools Integrate Security at Build and Runtime
item.description:
New AI Development Tools Integrate Security at Build and Runtime

As AI accelerates software development, hidden complexity has become a more critical security challenge. A new approach combining clean, curated base images, runtime profiling, and automated vulnerability remediation addresses this by reducing unnecessary code and exposure. Organizations continuously ingesting open source software must verify, trust, and evaluate components as they move through development, testing, and production following Zero Trust principles.

#AIsecurity #Containers #Vulnerabilities #CI/CD #ZeroTrust

Source: From Vulnerability Noise to Resilience: Rethinking Security in the AI Era

item.title: Pullrun Unifies Container and VM Execution with Single OCI Image Support
item.description:
Pullrun Unifies Container and VM Execution with Single OCI Image Support

Pullrun is a new AI development that collapses multiple execution engines into a single runtime, enabling the same OCI image to run as a container, Firecracker microVM, Apple Silicon VM, Kubernetes workload, or AI agent task. Modern infrastructure relies on disparate tools—Docker for development, containerd for production, Firecracker for isolation, and MCP agents for AI—each with separate image formats and storage models. Pullrun eliminates this fragmentation with a unified approach.

#containers #virtualization #oci #AIagents #firecracker #kubernetes

Source: pullrun/pullrun

item.title: Kubernetes Mutating Webhook Released for Automated Sidecar Injection
item.description:
Kubernetes Mutating Webhook Released for Automated Sidecar Injection

A new Kubernetes mutating webhook has been developed to automate the injection of sidecar containers into pod specifications. This tool simplifies the management of sidecars within a Kubernetes cluster.

🧩 How it works

To trigger an injection, users must add an annotation—defaulting to sidecar-injector.expedia.com/inject—to the target pod specification, including the name of the ConfigMap that defines the sidecar configuration.

⚙️ Key details

  • Sidecar Scope: Applications are limited to accessing sidecars within their own namespaces.
  • Namespace Watching: By default, the webhook monitors all namespaces except kube-system and kube-public.
  • Configurability: Namespace monitoring settings can be adjusted via Helm values.

🚀 Availability

Deployment is supported through two methods:

  • Helm: Files located in deployment/helm.
  • kubectl: Files located in deployment/kubectl.

To use the Helm method, users must add the repository to their Helm repositories. Those interested in contributing to the codebase are encouraged to review the developer documentation for building and testing procedures.

#Kubernetes #Sidecar #DevOps #Containers #Automation

Source: ExpediaGroup/kubernetes-sidecar-injector

item.title: Awesome‑Kubernetes List Published as GitBook Release
item.description:
Awesome‑Kubernetes List Published as GitBook Release

The community‑maintained Awesome‑Kubernetes repository has been packaged into a GitBook, allowing anyone to download and read the curated list as a book.

🔍 Overview

  • Kubernetes is an open‑source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications.
  • It groups containers that make up an application into logical units for easy management and discovery.
  • Kubernetes is known to be a descendant of Google’s system BORG.
  • The first unified container‑management system developed at Google was the system internally called Borg.
  • Borg was built to manage both long‑running services and batch jobs, which had previously been handled by two separate systems: Babysitter and the Global Work Queue.
  • The latter’s architecture strongly influenced Borg, but was focused on batch jobs; both predated Linux control groups.
  • Kubernetes celebrates its birthday every year on 21 July.
  • Kubernetes 1.0 was released on July 21 2015, after being first announced to the public at Dockercon in June 2014.

📚 Awesome‑Kubernetes Collection

  • A curated list for awesome kubernetes sources inspired by @sindresorhus’ awesome.
  • Without the help from these amazing contributors, building this awesome‑repo would never have been possible.
  • Thanks to Gitbook. This awesome list can now be downloaded and read in the form of a book.
  • Check it out → https://ramitsurana.gitbook.io/awesome-kubernetes/docs . Keep Learning Keep Sharing !!
  • If you see a package or project here that is no longer maintained or is not a good fit, please submit a pull request to improve this file.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The awesome‑kubernetes will now soon be available in the form of different releases and package bundles.
  • The release for awesome‑kubernetes 2015 bundle is released.

📦 Availability

  • The GitBook version can be downloaded directly from the linked URL.
  • Future bundles will allow downloading the awesome‑kubernetes release up to a certain period of time.

📜 Resources

Resource Author
Kubernetes Community Overview and Contributions Guide Ihor Dvoretskyi
An Intro to Google’s Kubernetes and How to Use It Laura Frank
Kubernetes: The Future of Cloud Hosting Meteorhacks
Kubernetes by Google Gaston Pantana
Key Concepts Arun Gupta
Application Containers: Kubernetes and Docker from Scratch Keith Tenzer
Learn the Kubernetes Key Concepts in 10 Minutes Omer Dawelbeit
The Children’s Illustrated Guide to Kubernetes Deis
The ‘kubectl run’ command Michael Hausenblas

💡 Why It Matters

  • Provides a single, community‑vetted source of Kubernetes learning material.
  • Encourages contributions and continuous updates through pull requests.
  • Makes the knowledge portable as a downloadable book, supporting offline learning.
  • Highlights the lineage from Google’s Borg system to modern Kubernetes practice.

#Kubernetes #OpenSource #GitBook #Containers

Source: ramitsurana/awesome-kubernetes
